# Install OpenCode in Chrome

## Outcome

Register `chrome` MCP in the user's chosen project, help the user complete Chrome pairing locally, and verify both MCP and browser readiness. Keep the conversation in OpenCode. The extension has no session picker or manual tab adoption.

## Workflow

1. Determine whether the user wants **project-local** or **global shared** access, and choose a permanent **extension checkout directory**. Global mode serves every OpenCode project with one daemon. Inspect existing `chrome` registration first; its `command` may identify an installed checkout. Preserve unrelated configuration and user files.
2. Check `node --version` (24+) and `opencode --version` (V2). If missing, guide installation from `https://nodejs.org/` and `https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/`. Do not guess V1 configuration shapes.
3. If no checkout exists, clone `https://github.com/asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome.git` into the chosen permanent directory. Read its README and SECURITY.md. If it already exists, inspect local changes before updating it.
4. From that checkout, run:

   ```sh
    npm run install:opencode -- --project "/absolute/path/to/target-project"
   ```

   For all projects, use `npm run install:opencode -- --global` instead. Do not combine `--global` and `--project`. On Windows, use `npm.cmd` if PowerShell blocks `npm`. The installer installs missing dependencies, generates/preserves private pairing settings, and registers MCP through OpenCode's CLI. Project-local mode copies this skill into the target project. Its output does **not** include the token or silently add approval rules.

5. If another bridge occupies the port, identify the owner and ask before disconnecting it. One extension connects to one bridge. Global mode uses `bridge/shared-main.js`; registering standalone `bridge/main.js` globally does not make it shared. Project-local entries override global configuration: ask before removing an obsolete local entry. Use `--port 8791` only when appropriate and update the popup URL. Stopping a shared daemon affects all its projects; never do so without authorization.
6. Run `npm run pair` from the checkout. This opens a **local, private pairing page**. Do not read its HTML, `.local/config.json`, or the clipboard into agent context. Do not screenshot that page. The user copies the token directly into the extension popup.
7. Guide the user through the Chrome-only steps: dedicated profile → `chrome://extensions` → Developer mode → Load unpacked → checkout's `extension/` → popup → URL/token → Save & enable browser → website permission. Do not claim these steps completed without confirmation.
8. Run `opencode mcp list` from the target project and `npm run doctor` from the checkout. Doctor prints only safe summaries. `--json` provides a machine-readable report; exit 0 means fully ready, exit 1 means attention needed. MCP connected is not proof Chrome is paired/enabled.
9. Offer to merge `examples/permissions.jsonc` into existing project permissions for supervised actions. Preserve rule order and explain later-rule/saved-approval effects. Never replace the entire config with the example.
10. Once ready, perform an authorized public-page smoke action: create a tab, read it, and report the observed result. Use actual MCP tools with OpenCode-supplied session metadata; never fabricate IDs or element refs.

## Multiple profiles

Chrome requires the extension to be installed/loaded separately in each participating regular profile. Use the same bridge URL and private pairing token, set a profile name in each popup, and choose Save & enable browser. New/unpaired profiles are not discoverable. Names and IDs are routing metadata, not proof of account identity.

Use `list_profiles` before account-sensitive browser work. When multiple profiles are registered, ask the user which to use and call `select_profile` with its returned ID. Do not choose another account because the intended profile is disconnected or disabled. Choices survive daemon restarts. Include `profileID` alongside explicit numeric `tabID` when multiple profiles exist, and pass the complete profile-scoped refs from snapshots unchanged. Disabling one profile does not affect the others.

After upgrading, restart the updated daemon, reload/name/enable each extension instance, and reconnect MCP adapters for the new tools. A legacy connection cannot distinguish multiple old profile copies; upgrade each copy. Never clone profile-local extension storage or clear saved routing history as a routine repair.

## Automatic local update activation

Shared mode can activate already-installed local runtime changes on next tool use after a one-time bootstrap of this mechanism: coordinate daemon restart, extension reload in each participating profile and MCP reconnect. Older running versions cannot safely bootstrap themselves. Later activation waits for all profiles to be idle, preserves pairing/ownership/account selection and announces tool-list changes; retained recordings/inspection defer it until normally finished/stopped/cancelled. Never discard captures, fetch Git code, install dependencies or approve permissions just to trigger activation. Legacy project-local mode and incompatible catalog clients still need manual reconnect/reload. See docs/updates.md for the expiring native-target checkpoint and manual disposable-profile smoke test. Do not inspect private checkpoints or reload production profiles as diagnostics.

## Tab cleanup

After extension changes, have the user reload the correct unpacked extension in each opted-in profile. No new permissions or pairing-token changes are required for tab cleanup. Inactive groups collapse after 15 minutes; manual collapse survives indicator refreshes. This uses browser activity, not OpenCode session-status polling or conversation-archive events.

Automatic closing is off by default. Do not enable it on the user's behalf during installation. If requested, explain that the popup's Archive after (hours) setting accepts 1–168 whole hours, defaults to 3, and saves automatically per profile. Already-enabled legacy profiles retain 24 hours until changed. Shortening the delay can close already-idle eligible tabs on the next check. Archiving saves URLs locally before closing eligible owned tabs, not unsaved forms or page state. Active, pinned, audible, loading, and Keep tabs are skipped; disconnected/disabled profiles never initiate cleanup. The popup offers Keep, Restore, and Delete saved URL. Restoration stays in the same connected/enabled profile. Do not inspect or export private archive URLs as installation diagnostics. See the checkout's README and SECURITY.md for limits and race caveats.

## Repairs

- **Chrome Errors shows Click target moved / iframe covered:** these are safe refusals, not evidence a click succeeded. The current worker catches page-operation exceptions inside injections and reports normal tool errors instead. Reload the updated extension worker, distinguish old Chrome error entries from new reproductions, and take a fresh snapshot after layout settles. Do not bypass guards or blindly retry side effects. A separate localhost WebSocket connection-refused entry means the daemon was unavailable at that moment; use doctor to check current readiness.

- **Chrome debugging banner flickers between clicks:** current code reuses the attachment and debounces idle detach for 30 seconds after successful ordinary clicks. Reload the updated extension worker to activate this; no new permissions or MCP catalog changes are required. Chrome's native banner cannot be hidden while attached. Cancel ends that attachment, while Disable this profile stops access; future explicit clicks can attach again after Cancel.

- **Missing keyboard/recording/inspection tools after upgrade:** the current catalog has 29 tools. Reload the extension in each opted-in profile (content version 10) and approve the added offscreen permission if prompted. A shared daemon must be restarted to load the new catalog; coordinate and obtain authorization before stopping it because every project/profile using it is interrupted. Reconnect MCP adapters afterward. Capture remains explicit; do not enable network bodies or start recording as an installation diagnostic on a private page. See docs/inspection.md and docs/recordings.md for profile-aware workflows, privacy limits, and the separate manual extension smoke test. Keyboard input requires a fresh single-use read_page.focus.token and a foreground owned tab; it never uses the clipboard, and literal TSV is not guaranteed multi-cell paste. See docs/keyboard.md; do not test writes against production sheets.

- **Page activity indicator is distracting:** click the orange dot, then Hide for this tab. To restore it, use Show page activity dot under that owned tab in the extension popup. This hides only the dot/status panel, not automation or its cursor; use Disable this profile to stop browser access. Chrome tab groups and the AI badge remain visible. There is no permanent page banner in the current extension; reload the correct unpacked extension if an old banner persists.

- **Missing script: setup:** commands ran in the target application. Run installation/setup from the extension checkout; MCP registration belongs in the target project.
- **Connection closed:** inspect `npm run doctor`, Node/bridge paths, dependencies, and port ownership. An older project's bridge may still run inside the OpenCode service after its terminal closes.
- **MCP connected but Chrome disconnected:** user checks profile, unpacked extension path, URL/token locally, and permission prompt; reconnect/reload as appropriate.
- **Timeout after an interaction:** inspect current page state before retrying; cancellation cannot undo a completed action.

Read the checkout's README for exact tools and recovery commands. No build step is required. Never commit `.local/`, pairing files, private browser data, or machine-specific credentials.

# OpenCode in Chrome — Chrome MCP server for browser automation

[![CI](https://github.com/asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

**OpenCode in Chrome** is a Chrome extension and local **Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for OpenCode**. Give your AI agent browser automation in your regular Chrome profile, with existing logins, session-owned tabs, and explicit multi-profile selection. Once paired and enabled, each OpenCode conversation can open and control its own tabs; the conversation stays in OpenCode.

[Install from source](#install-from-source-available-now) · [Guided setup prompt](#install-from-an-opencode-chat) · [Example workflow](#example-browser-automation-workflow) · [MCP tools](#tools) · [Security](SECURITY.md)

## Why use this Chrome MCP server?

- **Use existing logins.** New agent tabs use the Chrome profile you explicitly select. Cookies stay in Chrome; you do not need a separate headless-browser login for each task.
- **Keep conversations' tabs separate.** Agents control session-owned tabs, not your unrelated personal tabs. Chrome tab groups and an agent cursor show where automation is happening.
- **Choose the right account.** Opt in each Chrome profile once, then explicitly select the profile for each conversation. Disconnected or disabled profiles never fall back to another account.
- **Inspect and verify.** Read pages and accessible iframes, click controls, use guarded keyboard input, capture screenshots, inspect network/console activity, and export verified task walkthroughs.

The bridge runs locally with authenticated transport. Tab ownership is a targeting boundary, **not an account sandbox**: signed-in websites still have your account's permissions, browser actions need appropriate approval, and page data returned by tools can reach your model provider. Read the [security model](SECURITY.md) before using private accounts.

```text
OpenCode sessions → MCP stdio adapters → shared localhost bridge → extension → session-owned Chrome tabs
```

![Illustration of an orange session-owned tab group and independent OpenCode cursor](docs/assets/control-preview.svg)

_UI illustration, not a captured browser screenshot._

## Example browser automation workflow

After [setup](#install-from-source-available-now), try this read-only task in an OpenCode conversation:

```text
Use the Chrome MCP tools to open https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/ in a new
session-owned tab. If I have multiple Chrome profiles, ask which to use.
Find the MCP server setup documentation, summarize it, and include the source
URL. Do not change account settings, submit forms, or use my personal tabs.
Close only the tab you created when finished.
```

The workflow is **select profile → open an owned tab → read the page → follow snapshot refs → verify the result**. See the [agent quick start](#agent-quick-start) for tool-call examples. To capture an actual browser task as a shareable WebM, use the [verified recording workflow](docs/recordings.md); review it for private information before sharing.

[Install from source today](#install-from-source-available-now). The npm commands below still require package publication.

## Install from an OpenCode chat

Open an OpenCode conversation in the project where you want browser tools, then **copy and paste this prompt**:

```text

https://github.com/asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome

Do the setup for me, not just explain commands. Inspect existing chrome MCP
registration first. Reuse a suitable checkout, or clone the repo into a
permanent location. Preserve existing files, pairing settings, and unrelated
OpenCode configuration. Check that Node.js 24+ and OpenCode V2 are available.

Read the repo's README.md, SECURITY.md, and
.opencode/skills/install-opencode-in-chrome/SKILL.md, then follow the skill.
From the checkout, run the installer with --project pointing to this project's
absolute path. Use npm.cmd on Windows if needed. Investigate any port conflict;
ask before disconnecting another project's bridge or changing its settings.

Run npm run pair to open the private local pairing page. Never read the token,
the pairing HTML, or the clipboard into chat, logs, or screenshots. Guide me
through the Chrome steps you cannot perform: dedicated profile, Developer mode,
Load unpacked, toolbar pairing, and the website-permission prompt. Ask me to
confirm when those steps are complete, then continue setup and verification.

Check opencode mcp list from this project and npm run doctor from the checkout.
Only say setup is complete when MCP is connected and Chrome is connected and
enabled. Then use the Chrome MCP to open https://example.com in a new owned tab,
read it, and report the observed result. Do not invent session IDs or refs.
If blocked, explain the exact remaining step rather than claiming success.
```

The agent handles terminal commands, MCP registration, diagnostics, and final verification. **Chrome extension loading, pairing, and permission approval still require the user**; the prompt explicitly asks the agent to guide those steps and resume afterward. No token needs to be pasted into the conversation. If a prerequisite is missing, the agent should explain it and obtain permission before installing software or making system-wide changes.

See [installation prompt details](docs/install-prompt.md) for setup boundaries and expected results. The manual commands below remain available if you prefer doing the setup yourself.

## Inspect network, console and performance

Start `start_inspection` on an explicitly session-owned tab to read network requests/status/timing, redacted headers, opt-in text bodies, console logs and uncaught JavaScript errors. CPU profiling and main-frame performance timeline traces export private local files. Capture is bounded and shares its debugger attachment safely with clicks and recordings; no personal tabs, arbitrary CDP/evaluation, request interception or browser-wide trace are exposed. See [inspection tools, examples, privacy, and limits](docs/inspection.md).

## Record a verified task walkthrough

Chrome tools can now declare a task and immutable plan, record each step, discard failed attempts, and export an **edited WebM video plus a deterministic action manifest**. Use `start_recording` → `run_recording_step` → `finish_recording`; `cancel_recording` abandons a plan. Every step needs observable preconditions and postconditions, and final goal checks must pass before export. Files stay local under `.local/recordings/`; nothing is uploaded or replayed automatically.

This captures session-owned browser tabs, not the OpenCode terminal or full desktop. Removing mistakes from the walkthrough does not undo their side effects. Reload the extension to accept the new `offscreen` permission and reconnect `chrome` to discover the tools. See [recording workflow, examples, limits, and replay](docs/recordings.md).

## Package-runner install

The CLI is ready for npm publication as `@asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome`. The registry commands below become available after a maintainer publishes the package; pushing this repository does not publish it.

From the OpenCode project that should get browser tools:

```sh
npx @asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome install
```

Or with Bun installed:

```sh
bunx @asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome install
```

Both require **Node.js 24+, npm, Chrome 120+, and OpenCode V2**. Bun launches the Node CLI; it does not replace the bridge runtime. Do not pass `--bun`. The installer checks prerequisites, installs locked runtime dependencies without lifecycle scripts, registers `chrome` for the current directory, and opens private pairing instructions. It does not install Node or change your default runtime.

### Every session in every project

Install **global mode** once to make Chrome tools available to all OpenCode projects:

```sh
npx @asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome install --global
# Or:
bunx @asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome install --global
```

Registry commands still require npm publication. From a source checkout, global mode is available with:

```sh
npm run install:opencode -- --global
npm run pair
```

Global mode registers a lightweight MCP adapter in OpenCode's global configuration. Adapters from different projects automatically start or reuse **one authenticated localhost daemon**. Each opted-in Chrome profile pairs once with that daemon; switching projects does not require disconnecting Chrome. Profiles stay connected simultaneously, and each conversation controls only its own tabs in its selected profile. Global registration does not share conversation text or make personal tabs accessible.

For package-runner installs, the permanent directory is `opencode-in-chrome/global` under the same OS-specific user-data base listed below. The daemon starts on demand, survives individual adapter/session shutdown, and restarts before the next tool call or adapter connection if it stops. No launch agent or system service is installed. To stop it deliberately, run `npm run stop:shared` from its installation directory; this disconnects browser access for every project using it. Disconnect the adapters as well if you do not want the next call to start it again. A newly restarted bridge must wait for Chrome to reconnect; an early call may report Chrome disconnected. In-flight actions are cancelled, never replayed.

After the [one-time automatic-update setup](docs/updates.md), future local code updates activate on the next tool use: the adapter/catalog refreshes, and the shared daemon and changed extensions reload only after every connected profile is idle. Active or retained captures defer activation. Pairing, selected profiles, owned tabs and page data are preserved; no Git/npm download or permission approval is automatic. Older running versions still need one coordinated manual restart/reload/reconnect to load this mechanism.

**Migrating an existing project-local setup:** disconnect its old `chrome` MCP before reusing its port. After global registration, remove only the obsolete project-local `mcp.servers.chrome` entry, because local configuration overrides the global entry. Reconnect `chrome` and pair the extension with the global installation's URL/token using its private pairing page. The installer never kills an existing bridge, deletes local registrations, or changes Chrome pairing automatically. Use `--port 8791` if another application must keep the default port; one extension still connects to only one bridge at a time.

Options: `--global` or `--project "/absolute/path/to/project"`, `--port 8791`, and `--no-open`. `--global` and `--project` are mutually exclusive. On Windows, use `npx.cmd` if PowerShell blocks `npx`.

Without `--global`, the bridge and extension are copied to a permanent **per-project** installation, never registered from the npm/Bun cache:

- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/opencode-in-chrome/projects/<project-id>`
- Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\opencode-in-chrome\projects\<project-id>`
- Linux: `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode-in-chrome/projects/<project-id>` or `~/.local/share/opencode-in-chrome/projects/<project-id>`

Repeat installs reuse identical code and preserve pairing. If different code or unrecognized files already occupy the destination, installation stops rather than overwriting them. Upgrades currently require manually moving the old permanent installation aside after disconnecting its MCP and preserving its private `.local/` settings. If `chrome` is already configured from a checkout, keep using that checkout; the CLI will not silently replace it on first install. Each project still needs an available bridge port, and one extension instance connects to one bridge at a time.

Complete the pairing page's Chrome steps, then run `npm run doctor` from the printed installation directory. Browser readiness is separate from MCP connectivity.

## Automatic tab cleanup

The extension checks every 30 seconds while connected and enabled. After **15 minutes without browser-tool activity**, it collapses inactive session groups. Indicator refreshes preserve manual collapse, and grouping is serialized so concurrent events reuse one group per conversation/window. Existing duplicate groups are consolidated using owned tabs only; personal tabs are never adopted or closed.

In the extension popup, **Automatically archive eligible idle tabs** is **off by default**. Set **Archive after (hours)** to a whole number from **1–168**; changes save automatically per profile. The default is **3 hours**. Profiles that already enabled the previous fixed 24-hour rule keep **24 hours** on upgrade until you change it. Shortening the delay can archive already-idle tabs on the next 30-second check. Enabling archiving saves each eligible tab's URL/title in profile-local extension storage before closing it. Active, pinned, audible, loading, and **Keep** tabs are skipped, as are busy/paused sessions. Selecting an owned tab or navigating it resets its session's idle clock. Disconnected/disabled profiles never trigger cleanup. Restoring a saved URL requires this same profile to be connected and enabled. Use **Delete saved URL** to remove archive metadata. Archives are capped at 1,000 entries; cleanup stops rather than discarding older entries.

Active inspection sessions and retained recording plans also prevent idle cleanup between tool calls; finish or cancel them when no longer needed.

**Archiving preserves URLs only, not unsaved forms or page state.** Chrome does not reliably expose unsaved changes; enable automatic closing only if this tradeoff is acceptable. Closing is best effort: a user can change focus or page state between the final check and Chrome's close operation. Keep important tabs explicitly or pin them.

This is **browser inactivity**, not OpenCode session-status polling. It does not infer completion from a disconnect or automatically close tabs merely because a conversation becomes idle/archived. OpenCode session-event integration remains separate future work.

## Multiple Chrome profiles: opt in once per profile

**Chrome requires the extension to be installed in each participating profile.** Installing it in Work does not give it access to Personal. No Chrome profile directories or Google account identities are inspected.

1. In each profile you want to automate, open `chrome://extensions` and load the same checkout's `extension/` folder (or install the same extension distribution).
2. Open its popup and enter a friendly **Profile name**, such as **Work**, **Personal**, or **Testing**.
3. Pair using the same bridge URL and token from the private `npm run pair` page, then choose **Save & enable browser** and approve website access. This is that profile's opt-in; new/unpaired profiles are not exposed.
4. Repeat for other profiles. They connect to the same daemon/port without replacing each other. Each extension installation creates a persistent random ID in profile-local storage; labels are user-provided, not account authentication.

In OpenCode, ask: **“List my Chrome profiles and use Work for this conversation.”** The agent uses:

```text
select_profile {"profileID":"<Work's ID from list_profiles>"}
open_tab       {"url":"https://example.com"}
```

Choose a named profile explicitly once per conversation using `select_profile` (or pass `profileID` on its first browser call), even if only one is connected. With multiple registered profiles, ask the user which account/profile to use—even if another profile is disconnected. This avoids silently changing accounts for older conversations during migration. Choices are pinned per conversation and persisted across daemon restarts; **a disconnected or disabled selection never falls back to another account**. A lone legacy compatibility connection retains its old single-browser behavior until upgraded.

### Diagnose a port conflict on Windows

A confirmed failure mode is an older project's bridge still occupying `127.0.0.1:8790`. Starting another bridge on that port fails with `EADDRINUSE`; OpenCode may display only **Connection closed**. An older checkout can cause this even when the new MCP registration is correct.

In PowerShell, inspect the listener and its process (replace `8790` if you configured a different port):

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8790 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

# Substitute the OwningProcess number from the previous command.
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "ProcessId = <OwningProcess>" |
  Select-Object ProcessId, CommandLine
```

# Security model

## Tab cleanup and archives

Automatic closing is opt-in per Chrome profile. Archives contain URL/title/session metadata in trusted-context `chrome.storage.local`, not page contents or credentials fetched separately. URLs themselves can contain sensitive data; they are not synced by this extension, but remain accessible to the local Chrome user. Restore uses the same profile and requires browser access enabled. The popup can delete saved URLs. Never publish extension storage in diagnostics. Ownership is checked from the session binding, not group membership. Activity checks and close operations are not atomic; unsaved forms cannot be reliably detected and are not preserved. Session inactivity alone does not prove an agent has finished.

The archive delay is configurable per profile from 1 to 168 whole hours (default 3). Previously enabled fixed-delay profiles retain 24 hours on upgrade unless changed explicitly. Shortening it can close already-idle eligible tabs on the next check. Delay updates are validated and persisted before use, and cleanup rechecks the live delay before closing; invalid delays do not authorize closing. Changing the delay alone never enables automatic archiving.

This is a browser-automation prototype, not a sandbox for an untrusted agent. Session-owned tabs isolate **which tabs** an agent can manipulate. They do not isolate cookies, accounts, network access, or the privileges of the local OpenCode process.

## What could be dangerous?

| Risk                            | Example                                                                                                                     | What helps                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Signed-in account actions       | An agent opens your email, admin console, or shopping account in a new tab and submits a form                               | A dedicated Chrome profile; OpenCode tool permissions; supervision of write actions                 |
| Private-data disclosure         | Page text, input values, or screenshots are sent into the OpenCode conversation and may reach the configured model provider | Choose an appropriate provider; keep sensitive accounts out of the automation profile               |
| Prompt injection                | A page tells the model to ignore instructions, open another site, or transmit private information                           | Treat page text as untrusted data; constrain tasks and tool permissions; profile isolation          |
| Unintended side effects         | A click sends a message, deletes a record, approves a payment, or triggers a download                                       | Require approval for interaction tools when appropriate; cancellation cannot undo completed actions |
| Token compromise                | Another process or extension obtains the pairing token and impersonates a browser connection                                | Keep the token private; protect local files/profile; rotate it when exposed                         |
| Local/intranet access           | An owned tab visits a router, localhost application, or internal service                                                    | Use a restricted profile/environment and network controls where necessary                           |
| Dependency or update compromise | Modified extension/bridge code abuses its privileges                                                                        | Review code and updates; use lockfile installs; avoid loading untrusted forks                       |

The extension cannot reliably determine whether an arbitrary click is destructive. An orange cursor is visual feedback, **not an authorization check**. A website can also imitate a page indicator, so the page overlay is not a trusted security signal.

The activity dot is dismissible without revoking browser access; the Chrome tab group and AI extension badge remain ownership markers. Hiding it is not a stop/disable action. Content-script hide messages are restricted to their own verified owned tab, and the preference is stored with temporary ownership records. Only the dot/panel buttons intercept page pointer input; cursor/highlight layers remain pointer-transparent.

Page-operation guard exceptions are caught inside the injected function and rethrown as worker/tool failures, rather than uncaught extension-script errors. This changes reporting only: moved/covered/stale targets still fail closed, uncertain outcomes after a press remain explicit, and no automatic action retry, guessed-coordinate fallback, or guard bypass is added. Genuine bridge connection failures remain visible and should be diagnosed separately.

## Implemented safeguards

- **Loopback only:** the bridge listens on `127.0.0.1`, not a public interface.
- **Random shared token:** setup generates 32 random bytes. HTTP status reads require the token; WebSocket connections authenticate before receiving commands or replacing the connected browser. Tokens are not placed in URLs.
- **Host/origin checks:** unexpected hosts and ordinary website origins are rejected. Chrome-extension origins still need the token. The extension restricts the configured bridge URL to loopback HTTP.
- **Session ownership:** browser actions verify both session generation and owned tab ID. Existing personal tabs and other sessions' tabs cannot be targeted through the tools.
- **Profile opt-in and routing:** only paired extension installations are discoverable. Each regular Chrome profile stores its own random identity and enabled preference. Profile connections use separate ownership maps, command queues, pending results, and disable/disconnect handling. Conversation profile choices are persisted; an offline or disabled profile never causes fallback to another account. Profile-scoped refs and explicit profile checks on numeric tab IDs guard against cross-profile ambiguity. Simultaneous duplicate identities are rejected.
- **No arbitrary page evaluation tool:** model-visible tools are a fixed collection of tab and DOM operations. No shell command, filesystem API, cookie API, or arbitrary JavaScript evaluation is exposed by this MCP server.
- **Isolated-world execution:** injected content scripts use Chrome's default isolated world, separate from the page's JavaScript globals. Page content is returned as data.
- **Frame-scoped actions:** iframe refs encode the observed Chrome frame ID and resolve only within the owned tab. Document checks prevent reuse after frame navigation. Browser-level clicks map through intrinsic WindowProxy ancestry and validate containing-frame geometry/occlusion before mouse-down; page messages and DOM-supplied routing markers are not trusted. Inaccessible or unsupported frame geometry is rejected.
- **Trusted keyboard:** single-use profile/frame focus tokens guard owned foreground tabs, observed documents, editor/caret state, generation and cancellation. Clipboard/browser shortcuts are blocked; no clipboard is read or written. Input can submit or destroy data and still requires task authorization. Checks and dispatch are not atomic; uncertain outcomes must be inspected before retrying. `dispatched` never proves application acceptance or a saved spreadsheet cell. See [keyboard limitations](docs/keyboard.md).
- **Local update activation:** authenticated same-installation fingerprints and an all-profile idle barrier protect shared-mode restarts. Active/retained captures defer updates; actions are never replayed. A reload-only checkpoint in trusted local storage expires after 60 seconds and restores only matching native Chrome target IDs, not numeric tab IDs alone. It may contain sensitive URLs/titles and is consumed on startup; expiry prevents restoration but does not guarantee immediate deletion if reload fails. Never publish it. Updates do not fetch code, approve permissions or enable profiles. See [update safety and bootstrap limits](docs/updates.md).
- **Browser-level clicks:** the worker acquires a debugger lease only for a verified session-owned tab and sends fixed `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` commands. Content scripts hit-test the ref before input and again after mouse movement; stale, disabled, moved, or covered targets fail closed. Successful ordinary clicks retain an otherwise-idle attachment for a 30-second debounced grace period, reducing Chrome-banner churn without enabling data capture. Ownership/generation/enabled checks still apply on every acquisition. Disable/disconnect, pause, closure, protected navigation, or Chrome's Cancel clear the attachment without waiting for the timer; acquired click failures and explicit final recording/inspection releases do not use the grace period. Other authorized capture leases can keep a shared attachment active. Tools never expose arbitrary CDP commands. Input dispatch is not proof of application acceptance.
- **Credential storage separation:** extension local/session storage is restricted to trusted extension contexts. Injected content scripts cannot read the stored pairing token.
- **No password values in snapshots:** native password-input values are excluded. This does not guarantee that all secrets on a page are concealed; other inputs, page text and screenshots can contain sensitive data.
- **Disable control:** disabling access rejects bridge work, invalidates generations, and notifies owned-page content scripts to stop pending interactions.
- **Disconnect handling:** losing the bridge connection suspends browser actions and invalidates queued work. Reconnection rechecks enabled settings and browser permissions before announcing readiness.
- **Authenticated readiness:** pairing and reconnection leave controls suspended until the bridge acknowledges authentication. Invalid ownership data in a new handshake is rejected before replacing a working connection.
- **Cancellation propagation:** MCP cancellation and action timeouts are forwarded to the extension. Queued commands and pending pre-click animations can be cancelled. Completed actions are not reversed; Chrome API calls already in progress may still finish.
- **Expiry/stale refs:** browser commands expire after 25 seconds; element refs are scoped to a document/snapshot and checked again before delayed interactions.
- **Private local state:** `.local/` is ignored by Git. The bridge token and machine-specific MCP configuration must never be committed.
- **Credential-safe onboarding:** `install:opencode` and `doctor` do not print tokens. `pair` writes an ignored, restricted local HTML page with copy/reveal controls and no remote resources. That page contains a credential; keep it out of agent reads, screenshots, and shared files. The lower-level `setup` command intentionally prints the token for manual setup.
- **Release boundaries:** standalone and extension-only archives use an explicit source allowlist and exclude `.local/`, `node_modules/`, and Git state. Releases include checksums; verify downloads from the maintainer's repository.
- **Package-runner installation:** npm packages use an explicit file allowlist and a publishable lockfile. The CLI copies code into a permanent per-project directory, installs locked runtime dependencies with lifecycle scripts disabled, and refuses to overwrite different existing code. Package-runner caches are never the registered bridge location. npm/Bun may separately apply their own dependency-install behavior when fetching the CLI.
- **Global shared mode:** one per-user daemon accepts authenticated localhost tool calls from multiple project adapters. Calls require the pairing token, reject browser origins, validate fixed tool schemas and session metadata, and limit request bodies to 128 KiB. Adapters never launch duplicate listeners intentionally, stop unrelated processes, or retry completed actions. Stopping the daemon affects all projects. The same local-user and forged-session-metadata limitations still apply.

## Inspection privacy

Network/console capture requires an explicit `start_inspection` on a session-owned HTTP/HTTPS tab. Bodies are not retained/read by default and require two opt-ins. Fixed Network/Runtime/Log/Page/Profiler commands are used; no arbitrary CDP, heap evaluation, interception or cookie/storage-reading API is exposed. Events from child protocol sessions are ignored. The shared debugger lease manager enforces ownership/generation boundaries and cancels/detaches on disable, disconnect or tab removal.

Captured headers, URLs, common labelled secrets and nested JSON fields are redacted; unknown header values are hidden. This is not complete secret/PII redaction. Requests/logs remain bounded in memory, expire after five minutes and are cleared on navigation/stop. CPU profiles and main-frame PerformanceObserver traces export generated private files under ignored `.local/inspections/`; raw profiles are not returned into model context. Review all returned content and files before sharing. Captured page/network/log data is untrusted and must never be treated as instructions.

Performance timeline capture uses a fixed bundled isolated-world helper, not browser-wide Chromium tracing. Only supported main-frame timeline entries are collected, and CPU sampling uses the attached target's VM. No extra extension permission is requested. See [inspection](docs/inspection.md) for scope, exclusions and limits.

## Recording privacy

Recordings are explicit, session-scoped, and limited to an owned tab. The debugger sends fixed screencast/screenshot/ack commands; an offscreen extension document uses WebCodecs to encode only verified segments. No desktop, microphone, personal-tab capture, arbitrary CDP, or arbitrary evaluation tool is added. Captured pixels, typed literals, page URLs, and selectors can still disclose private information. There is no automatic redaction: review local artifacts before sharing them.

Exports use generated paths beneath ignored `.local/recordings/`, private POSIX permissions, and inherited Windows ACLs. Video bytes are stripped from MCP responses; only artifact paths and safe summaries reach the model. Failed attempts are omitted and counted, not erased from application history or rolled back. Observable checks verify the declared page state, not external effects. Replay requires an explicit new tool workflow and can repeat side effects.

The added `offscreen` permission enables a bundled hidden encoder document; it does not request screen-sharing or microphone access. Encoding and capture are bounded, cancelled on disable/disconnect, and limited to authenticated extension messages and session-owned tabs. Previously exported files are never deleted automatically.

Inspection/recording state is local to each opted-in Chrome profile and session; changing the conversation's profile never retargets existing capture or reads. A profile switch alone does not cancel previously authorized capture: stop/cancel first, or return explicitly to the original profile to stop it (inspection expires after five minutes). Active inspection and retained recording plans block idle tab cleanup. Artifact responses identify their profile without passing routing metadata into strict artifact payload schemas. Post-export recording cleanup includes the original profile ID so a concurrent selection change cannot clear a recording in a different profile.

`run_recording_step` is a macro that executes the plan's browser actions inside the extension. OpenCode approval applies to the macro, not to separate nested click/type calls. Require approval for `chrome_run_recording_step` when using supervised actions; the supplied `chrome_*` ask rule already covers it. Existing custom rules for individual interaction tools alone do not. The feature does not modify user permission rules or saved approvals.

## Trust boundaries and limitations

1. The model and webpages are not trusted to make safe decisions automatically.
2. The OpenCode process, MCP client, bridge, extension, local user account and installed code are trusted. OpenCode session IDs are routing metadata, not authentication credentials. A malicious local MCP client can forge this metadata; session ownership is not a multi-user authorization system.
3. New tabs share the normal cookies and login state of the Chrome profile containing the extension. Opening an authenticated page can have side effects even before a click.
4. Browser website permission is broad (`<all_urls>`), including permissions needed for viewport captures. Application-level ownership restricts tool targets, but the installed extension remains powerful.
5. Other OpenCode servers/tools, such as shell or network tools, are outside this extension's controls. An agent with shell access can use the privileges of your OS account independently of these browser tools.
6. Disconnect/disable/cancellation are best-effort stop mechanisms, not transactional rollback or a network firewall. They cannot stop a request that has already been sent.
7. The token is stored as local data, not encrypted by the extension. POSIX setup uses mode `0600`; on Windows, effective protection comes from the directory's inherited NTFS ACLs. Malicious software running as your user is outside this threat model.
8. Chrome extensions in an incognito profile or across separate Chrome profiles are not managed by this connection unless separately installed and paired.
9. Viewport capture uses Chrome's active-tab API. The extension verifies the target before and after capture, but this is a best-effort race check: avoid switching tabs during screenshots. It is not an atomic tab-specific capture API.
10. The required `debugger` permission is powerful and can access more than mouse input; the extension's implementation limits its use, not the Chrome permission itself. Chrome may show a debugging banner, and DevTools or enterprise policy may block attachment. DOM validation and input dispatch are not atomic: the page may change between them. Cancellation after mouse-down cannot undo a handler or webhook that already ran; inspect state before retrying.
11. Snapshots may include cross-origin iframe content wherever Chrome grants script access. Treat embedded page content as untrusted too; private embedded forms or account data may reach the model provider. The same tab-ownership and profile/account limitations apply to frames. Frame geometry validation is best effort and does not make input dispatch atomic.
12. Profile IDs and labels are routing metadata, not authentication or proof of Google/account identity. Names are user-provided and untrusted as instructions. All profile connections share the local pairing secret; trusted local software with that secret can impersonate a profile. Do not clone profile-local extension storage. Incognito is not a separate supported profile identity. Disabling a profile stops automation, but does not delete its metadata or session-selection history.
13. `.local/profile-routing.json` contains profile labels/IDs and conversation selections, not pairing tokens or page contents. It is written atomically (POSIX mode `0600`) and ignored by Git. Corrupt or unwritable routing state fails closed rather than resetting selections or sending browser actions. Deliberately deleting this file resets routing history; do not do so as a routine troubleshooting step.

## Recommended deployment

For initial installation, use a **dedicated Chrome profile** containing only accounts you intend to automate. This retains the useful signed-in browsing behavior while avoiding access to unrelated personal/work accounts.

Review tool permissions in OpenCode. For sensitive work, use `ask` for interaction tools (`chrome_click`, `chrome_type`, `chrome_select`, `chrome_check`) and navigation. Approvals happen in OpenCode's normal interface, not a chat drawer in the extension. The extension does not silently modify your OpenCode permission rules.

A ready-to-merge [supervised permission example](examples/permissions.jsonc) asks for all browser actions except listing, reading, and scrolling. Rules use OpenCode V2's ordered `permissions` array. The MCP registration name determines the action prefix; update `chrome_` if you register under a different name.

Keep the bridge on localhost, keep the token out of repositories/logs/screenshots, and disable browser access in the toolbar popup when finished. Session-created tabs remain open when disabled, but the agent cannot manipulate them through this server until re-enabled.

## Rotate an exposed token

```sh
npm run setup -- --rotate-token
```

Then reconnect `chrome` in OpenCode's `/mcps` interface and replace the saved token in the extension popup. Rotation changes the file; an already-running bridge retains its previous token until restarted. Do not paste the token into a GitHub issue or an OpenCode prompt.

## Reporting vulnerabilities

Private vulnerability reporting is enabled. Report suspected vulnerabilities through [GitHub's private reporting form](https://github.com/asaf-labs/opencode-in-chrome/security/advisories/new). Do not post pairing tokens, signed-in page contents, screenshots with private information, or working exploit details in a public issue before coordinating a fix.

Repository admin access is required to manage private reporting and branch protection. See [maintainer setup](docs/maintainer-setup.md) for the configured safeguards and maintenance instructions. If the private reporting form is unavailable, establish a private channel with the maintainer rather than posting confidential details publicly.

This prototype has not undergone an independent security audit. Automated tests verify the implemented boundaries; they do not establish that browser automation is safe for every account or task.

# Architecture

```text
OpenCode conversation
  └─ MCP stdio (session ID in ai.opencode/sessionID metadata)
      └─ stdio adapter → shared Node daemon, bound to 127.0.0.1
          └─ authenticated WebSocket /browser, protocol version 3 per opted-in profile
              └─ Chrome service worker
                  └─ session-owned tabs + isolated-world content scripts
```

It copies the reusable installation skill into the target project's `.opencode/skills/` directory and refuses to overwrite a differing skill.

With `--global`, it registers `bridge/shared-main.js` globally and does not write a project-local skill. Package-runner installations use one user-wide permanent directory in global mode and per-project directories otherwise. The installed daemon path is always permanent, never the package-runner cache.

`scripts/pair.js` creates a private local pairing page from validated configuration. It opens through the operating system's default browser launcher with no shell interpolation. The user transfers the token into Chrome directly. `scripts/doctor.js` uses `diagnostics.js` for safe human/JSON reports; it does not log response bodies, account URLs, or tokens. `bridge/listen.js` supplies actionable startup errors for occupied ports and denied listeners.

## Connection lifecycle

Shared-mode `shared-main.js` is a stable MCP supervisor. `RefreshingAdapter` starts `shared-adapter.js` in a fresh process on runtime-fingerprint changes at an idle request boundary and announces a new tool catalog. The adapter checks the daemon revision on next use. Authenticated `/activate` compares installation/daemon identity, closes admission, and prepares every connected profile before committing reloads and stopping the old daemon. Source races, missing support, active commands, retained captures and persistence failures defer or fail closed. Only pre-dispatch maintenance is retried; browser tool requests are never replayed.

`ExtensionUpdates` checks private worker busy/capture state, checkpoints native target identities for 60 seconds when reload is needed, and restores only matching existing tabs after session-storage clearing. The loaded extension fingerprint also scopes content-helper injection so unchanged manual content-version numbers cannot keep stale helpers alive. Profile routing stays in its existing durable file; pairing, enabled state and archives are unchanged. See [automatic update activation](updates.md) for bootstrap, catalog-client and permission limitations.

1. The worker restricts storage to trusted extension contexts and restores session-owned tabs from `chrome.storage.session`. It starts suspended and invalidates old generations.
2. It connects to the configured loopback URL, rechecks website permission, and sends `hello` with the token, enabled preference, and ownership bindings.
3. The bridge checks host/origin, authenticates the token, and validates all ownership bindings before replacing a connected browser. It replies `ready`.
4. Only after `ready` echoes the expected profile ID does the worker enable controls. Named profiles use protocol 3 while browser access is enabled; protocol 2 is retained for a single legacy compatibility connection.
5. Disconnect suspends page controls, changes generations, rejects pending bridge calls, and schedules reconnection. Pairing changes also suspend controls before reconnecting.

Both modes support multiple authenticated browser-profile connections. In global mode, every project gets a stdio MCP adapter, and all adapters forward authenticated HTTP `/call` requests to one daemon. Concurrent startup attempts rely on exclusive loopback port binding: one daemon wins, and all adapters reuse its authenticated status. A mismatched token, standalone listener, or unrelated process is never terminated or replaced.

`bridge/profiles.js` maintains one `BrowserHub` per profile, isolates socket messages/results, and pins each conversation to a profile. The popup's protocol-3 handshake carries a persistent random profile ID and user label; protocol-2 extensions share one legacy compatibility connection. `bridge/profile-store.js` persists profile labels and conversation selections in the config directory's `profile-routing.json`, using serialized atomic writes and restrictive POSIX permissions. Reconnection of a different profile does not alter an existing selection, and offline/disabled selections never fall back. Commands wait for durable selection state; storage failure blocks actions. Profile selection cannot change during in-flight browser work. Named-profile refs add an outer `p<profileID>:` scope around the existing frame ref, and explicit numeric tab targets require matching profile context when profiles can overlap.

The daemon validates session metadata, fixed tool names and input schemas, and a 128 KiB request-body limit. Closing an adapter does not stop the daemon. Cancelling a call aborts its HTTP request; the response-close event aborts the corresponding BrowserHub action and forwards cancellation to Chrome. There is no automatic action retry. An authenticated `/shutdown` endpoint cancels pending work, closes Chrome, and stops the listener. Each new tool call checks daemon availability before dispatch, and the next call or adapter startup launches a fresh daemon if needed. The extension can restore session-owned bindings on reconnect; an early call fails safely until Chrome connects.

## Commands, cancellation, and refs

The content script's activity UI is separate from authorization. Chrome groups and the AI action badge remain persistent ownership markers; the page has no permanent banner. The main-frame dot appears during content actions, expands on click, and can be hidden per owned tab. Dot visibility is saved alongside temporary ownership records and applied before page actions and after navigation. Content-script messages may only hide the dot for their own verified owned tab; popup controls can show it again. Cursor/highlight layers stay pointer-transparent and fade when idle, independent of the dot. Only dot/panel buttons accept clicks, and shadow UI is excluded from page snapshots.

The bridge attaches a random request ID, session generation, and 25-second deadline. The worker queues commands per session; different sessions can run concurrently. SessionBrowser checks ownership and generation before work and after asynchronous boundaries. Content actions recheck enabled state, cancellation, snapshot revision, and DOM validity after the cursor animation before interaction.

`read_page` creates a fresh ref map. A monotonically increasing ref counter avoids accidentally reusing old names; snapshot revision checks also stop a pending action when a new snapshot replaces its map. Document IDs and URL checks prevent refs crossing documents or same-document navigation.

Snapshots now discover standard interactive ARIA roles, including custom multiselect options. Open popup controls are prioritized within each frame's 300-element cap. `extension/frame-refs.js` scopes child refs as `f<Chrome-frame-ID>:e<local-ref>` and combines snapshots without losing frame identity. A read of one frame refreshes only its refs; default reads cover all accessible frames. SessionBrowser tracks document IDs separately for each observed frame, without persisting stale routing across navigation or suspension.

Iframe mouse input remains a main-viewport browser action. Content scripts derive the frame's ancestry through cross-origin-safe WindowProxy identity, not page messages or DOM markers. Before pressing, the worker revalidates the target and projects its point through each containing frame, including borders and positive axis-aligned scaling. Each ancestor is hit-tested. Missing, navigated, covered, moved, or unsupported transformed frames fail closed. No new Chrome permission is required beyond existing script access and debugger input.

For `click`, the content script prepares viewport CSS coordinates from a visible, unobstructed client rectangle without calling `el.click()`. The worker validates the original ref, document, snapshot/control revisions, and hit target, acquires a debugger lease on the owned tab, and dispatches mouse movement. It revalidates after hover handlers before sending press/release, checks cancellation/generation/expiry between operations, and releases the lease in cleanup. A successful ordinary click debounces final detach for 30 seconds; authorized inspection/recording can retain the attachment with live leases. Attachment failures never fall back to DOM clicks. The result is `{ tabID, dispatched: true, applicationAccepted: null }`, not an application-state assertion. Once a press is attempted, errors warn that the page may already have changed; no retry is automatic. DOM validation and browser input remain separate operations, so page changes can still race dispatch.

MCP cancellation and timeouts send `cancel` to the worker. Queued work is marked cancelled; executing page interactions receive an extension message. Disable and disconnect notify all owned tabs. These are best-effort stops, not rollback: an already-issued Chrome call or network request may complete.

Bundled page actions, click/frame validation, recording conditions, and performance helpers catch their own exceptions inside the injected function, returning a small `opencodeError` envelope. The worker converts that envelope back to a normal tool failure. This avoids leaking expected refusals into Chrome's uncaught extension-error reporting while retaining the original message, cancellation/cleanup, pre-press guards, and post-press uncertain-outcome warning. Transport/permission/injection failures still reject normally. `test/page-errors.test.js` executes the actual injected callbacks in isolated VM contexts; the real-Chrome click regression also checks that a covered-target refusal does not escape as a script-evaluation exception.

## Persistence and trust

### Idle tab maintenance

The worker's 30-second reconnect alarm also schedules `TabLifecycle.sweep`. Maintenance runs only while the profile is connected/enabled, skips busy or paused sessions, and serializes with browser commands per session. Browser commands, owned-tab activation/navigation, and inherited tabs update the session's activity timestamp. Missing timestamps get a fresh grace period on worker restoration; inactivity is not proof that OpenCode has finished a conversation. There is no OpenCode session-status polling or conversation-archive event integration.

Retained recording plans and active inspection sessions also prevent idle cleanup between tool calls. Nested recorded actions use the parent step's session lock rather than recursively acquiring it. Explicit recording cancellation and inspection stop bypass the command queue/lock so they can interrupt pending attachment or capture.

After 15 minutes, inactive groups can collapse unless they contain active or non-owned tabs. Group marking is serialized per session and consolidates only verified owned tabs within each window; indicator updates never force groups open. With explicit popup opt-in, eligible tabs can be archived after the profile's configured `archiveAfterHours` delay (1–168 whole hours). The new default is 3; migration preserves 24 hours for profiles that had already opted into the old fixed rule. Settings mutations are serialized, validated, and persisted before the live cleanup preference changes. The sweep reads the current delay again before closing, so increasing it during archive persistence can prevent a close; invalid delays fail closed. Active, pinned, audible, loading, and Keep tabs are excluded. URL/title/session metadata is saved before removal, eligibility and ownership are checked again, and persistence failure prevents closing. These checks and Chrome removal are not atomic; unsaved page state cannot be detected reliably or restored.

Archives remain in the same Chrome profile. Restore creates an owned tab using the recorded session and current generation, requires the profile to be connected/enabled, and removes the saved record after opening. The popup can delete records without restoring them. Archive storage is capped at 1,000 entries; cleanup stops rather than evicting history. Crashes or uncertain closes can leave both a live tab and a saved URL. See [automatic cleanup](../README.md#automatic-tab-cleanup) and [security notes](../SECURITY.md#tab-cleanup-and-archives).

### Storage locations

- `.local/config.json`: token and port; ignored by Git.
- `.local/profile-routing.json`: opted-in profile IDs/labels and durable conversation selections; ignored by Git.
- `.local/mcp-config.json`: generated machine-specific OpenCode registration; ignored by Git.
- `chrome.storage.local`: pairing, profile identity/name, enabled/auto-archive preferences, and `tabArchives` URL/title/session records; restricted to trusted contexts and never synchronized across profiles.
- `chrome.storage.session`: temporary ownership, current tab, group IDs, generations, last activity, and Keep flags; cleared by a Chrome browser restart. Persistent URL archives do not restore ownership of existing tabs after that restart.
- Bridge memory: pending requests, routing bindings, and the last 100 activity summaries.

Session ownership is a tab-targeting boundary, not account isolation. Session IDs are trusted MCP routing metadata, not credentials. Page content is untrusted data. See [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md) for the complete threat model.

## Tab inspection

`bridge/inspection-tools.js` defines opt-in inspection and bounded network/console/profile tools. `extension/inspections.js` scopes event buffers to session/tab/generation, sanitizes captured metadata and invalidates IDs on navigation. `inspection-profiles.js` uses fixed CPU profiler commands and a bundled isolated-world PerformanceObserver helper, not global Chromium tracing. `inspection-privacy.js` bounds and redacts output.

See [inspection contract](inspection.md).

Only successful ordinary clicks request debounced release: when no other leases remain, schedule detach for 30 seconds later. The next acquisition cancels that timer and the next successful final click release resets it. A timer token prevents stale callbacks from closing a reacquired/new entry. Live leases always prevent idle detach; explicit inspection/recording releases and acquired click failures close the final attachment immediately. Clear/detach events cancel idle timers; suspend starts clearing before awaiting storage/UI work. No capture domains are enabled by retaining an idle click attachment. `test/debugger-sessions.test.js` covers debounce boundaries, reuse, live capture leases, safety cleanup, stale timers, and invalid generations/ownership.

The common tool layer adds profile routing to all 29 tools. Profile metadata is separated from strict artifact payload validation, then included in path/summary responses; recording cleanup after persistence carries its original profile ID. Captures never migrate when a conversation selects another Chrome profile. Stop/cancel before switching, or select the original profile explicitly to access retained data. Existing iframe action routing, pointer validation, per-tab activity-dot preferences, and configurable tab cleanup remain independent of capture.

`TrustedKeyboard` reuses debugger leases for `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` and `Input.insertText`. Content version 10 keeps private focus/editor observations; snapshots expose only focus metadata and a single-use token. Frame/profile layers scope the token, and the worker validates foreground ownership, document, focus/caret state, generation and cancellation before input. Chords use an allowlist with reverse key-up cleanup and no retries or clipboard APIs. Results distinguish dispatch from application acceptance. These tools are not recording-plan actions; see [keyboard workflow and limits](keyboard.md).

# Network, console and performance inspection

Inspection is explicit and restricted to a session-owned HTTP/HTTPS tab. It does not adopt personal tabs, attach child targets, intercept requests, expose arbitrary CDP, evaluate arbitrary page code, or read cookies/storage directly. The debugger permission already used for guarded clicks is sufficient; no additional manifest permission is added.

## Workflow

First call `list_profiles` and `select_profile` for the intended Chrome account/profile. All inspection tools accept `profileID`; include the selected profile's ID with explicit `tabID` when multiple profiles are registered. Inspection remains attached to its original profile/tab, never follows a profile selection, and is not automatically stopped just by switching the conversation's profile. Stop it before switching, or explicitly select the original profile to stop it later. Its five-minute expiry still applies; disabling/disconnecting the original profile discards its captures. Active inspection sessions are excluded from idle tab cleanup.

1. Use `open_tab`/`list_tabs` to get the explicit owned `tabID`.
2. Call `start_inspection({ tabID })` before reproducing the issue. Historical console messages and traffic are not returned. Set `captureBodies: true` only if reading potentially sensitive request/response content is authorized.
3. Reproduce using existing browser tools or manual interaction.
4. Read `network_requests({ tabID, urlContains, limit })` and `console_logs({ tabID, level, limit })`.
5. Inspect an exact returned request UUID with `network_request({ tabID, requestID })`. Headers are redacted. Bodies require **both** `captureBodies: true` at start and `includeBody: true` here; `maxBodyChars` bounds returned text.
6. Optionally profile the same tab with the start/stop tools below.
7. Call `stop_inspection({ tabID })` to discard in-memory captures and release its debugger lease. It never closes the tab or deletes previously exported files.

Example:

```js
// profileID and tabID must come from this conversation's selected profile and owned tabs.
await chrome.start_inspection({ profileID, tabID: 123, captureBodies: true });
// Reproduce on this tab using its browser tools.
await chrome.network_requests({ profileID, tabID: 123, urlContains: '/api/', limit: 20 });
await chrome.console_logs({ profileID, tabID: 123, level: 'warning', limit: 20 });
// Use an actual requestID returned above, never invent one.
await chrome.network_request({ profileID, tabID: 123, requestID, includeBody: true });
await chrome.stop_inspection({ profileID, tabID: 123 });
```

These illustrate MCP inputs, not standalone JavaScript imports. In OpenCode Code Mode, discover and call the corresponding `tools.chrome` tools.

## Network data

Requests include redacted URLs, methods, resource types, HTTP status, total duration, and available DNS/connect/wait timing. HTTP 4xx/5xx responses are `completed`, not transport failures. Redirect hops get distinct public request IDs; a previous hop cannot return the final hop's body. Request and response header metadata can be incomplete due to protocol event ordering, cache behavior, or eviction.

Response bodies are read from Chrome's existing capture buffer using a fixed protocol command; they are never re-fetched. Binary, oversized, evicted, pending, failed, redirected, or unavailable captures return an explicit state/reason rather than guessed data. Request bodies are retained only with opt-in. File uploads and multipart data are not reconstructed. WebSocket messages, service-worker background targets, and out-of-process iframe targets are not captured. Tab-target traffic may include resources from same-process frames within that tab.

Document changes clear old requests and logs, discard profiles, and invalidate old request IDs. The incoming navigation's request is preserved when its loader is identifiable. Inspection remains attached for the new page until stopped, except protected-page navigation ends it. Same-document navigation also clears retained data.

## Console data

`console_logs` includes console calls, browser log entries, and uncaught exceptions, with level filtering and available source location. Selecting a level includes more severe levels. Strings and primitive values are bounded; errors include their description, but ordinary objects are represented by type placeholders. No getters, object properties, or heap state are evaluated. Clear-console calls do not erase the diagnostic buffer. Duplicate browser/protocol reports of an error may appear.

## CPU profiles

Call `start_cpu_profile({ tabID, durationMs: 10000 })`, reproduce the workload, then `stop_cpu_profile({ tabID })`. Sampling uses a fixed 1 ms interval and automatically stops at the deadline, up to 30 seconds. The stop tool also retrieves an already auto-completed profile.

The bridge saves a generated private `.local/inspections/<UUID>/profile.cpuprofile` and returns only its path, summary, and routing `profileID`. Import the file into Chrome DevTools' JavaScript profiler or compatible tooling. Function names/URLs are sanitized; raw samples do not enter model context through the MCP response. Profiling is scoped to the attached tab target's JavaScript VM, not the system or other debugging targets.

## Performance timeline traces

Call `start_performance_trace({ tabID, durationMs: 10000 })`, reproduce the workload, then `stop_performance_trace({ tabID })`. A bundled isolated-world helper observes supported main-frame performance entries: marks, measures, long tasks, navigation, paint, layout shifts, and resource timings. Unsupported entry types are reported in artifact metadata, and events predating the start are excluded.

Exports are private `.local/inspections/<UUID>/timeline.json` files in Chrome trace-event JSON format, labelled `main-frame-performance-observer`. They include relative microsecond timestamps, durations and bounded numeric details, suitable for compatible trace viewers such as Perfetto.

**This is not a full Chromium renderer/system trace.** Browser-wide `Tracing.start` is deliberately not exposed: it can collect unrelated tabs/processes. GPU, browser internals, network payloads, screenshots, and complete engine scheduling are not part of this timeline. Navigation generally finishes before inspection starts, so its already-completed navigation entry is not backfilled. Resource/mark names can still contain private content.

Each profile is retained for retry if file persistence fails. After retrieving it, a new explicit start replaces that profile. Stop inspection to discard both profiles and all captured data.

## Limits, cleanup and privacy

- At most three inspected tabs, each with a five-minute capture window.
- Up to 200 request records within a 2 MiB metadata budget; evictions are counted.
- Up to 300 console entries, each 2,000 characters; reads return at most 100 messages/requests and report truncation.
- Chrome's network body buffers are bounded to 2 MiB total / 128 KiB per resource. Returned body text is at most 20,000 characters. Availability is best effort.
- CPU/performance capture is at most 30 seconds; CPU profiles allow at most 10,000 nodes / 60,000 samples, performance timelines 1,000 entries, and an exported artifact at most 5 MiB.
- Stop, disable, disconnect, session generation changes, tab closure, protected-page navigation, and debugger detachment discard affected inspection data. Navigation discards profiles but continues inspection on HTTP/HTTPS pages.
- A debugger lease manager coordinates inspection, verified recording and guarded clicks. Stopping one does not detach a debugger still used by another. DevTools attachment conflicts fail without fallback or taking over another debugger.
- Successful ordinary clicks keep an idle attachment for a 30-second debounced grace period to reduce Chrome-banner flicker. Starting inspection reuses that attachment, but never starts capture implicitly; explicit inspection stop still releases its final lease immediately. Disable/disconnect or Chrome's Cancel do not wait for the grace period.
- The performance helper has its own bounded timer. All capture state is in memory; worker restarts do not resume it. Exported files remain local, ignored by git and excluded from packages/releases.
- Standard authorization/cookie/secret headers are redacted; unknown header values are also redacted. Common sensitive query parameters, nested JSON fields and labelled console secrets are masked. URL credentials/fragments are removed. This is **best-effort redaction**, not a guarantee: page text, endpoint paths, unlabelled secrets and user data can still be sensitive. Inspect files before sharing.
- POSIX directories/files use private permissions; Windows inherits NTFS ACLs. Artifact names/paths are generated by the bridge and no upload happens automatically.

## Activation and tests

Reload the unpacked extension in each opted-in profile and reconnect `chrome` to discover the nine inspection tools (**29 total** including trusted keyboard input, verified recordings and profile routing). Recording also adds the `offscreen` permission; accept updated permissions if Chrome prompts. In global shared mode, coordinate `npm run stop:shared` from the installation directory before reconnecting; adapter reconnection alone does not reload the running daemon. This affects every project and connected profile using that daemon. No configuration, approvals or live bridge are changed by tests.

After [one-time automatic-update setup](updates.md), subsequent local shared-mode updates activate on next use only when all profiles are idle. Retained inspection/recording state blocks activation until stopped/exported/cancelled normally; it is never discarded just to update. The manual procedure remains the fallback for bootstrap, missing permissions and incompatible clients.

`npm run check` exercises ownership, schema bounds, redaction, navigation/redirects, body opt-in, eviction, cancellation races, shared debugger leases, artifact privacy and MCP output stripping. The isolated real-Chrome regression verifies actual network/console events, uncaught errors, response bodies, CPU samples and performance timeline events:

```sh
CHROME_BINARY="/path/to/chrome" npm run test:browser
```
